title: In its season
hook: figs come in season and go, and so do the people we love

segments.voice: Yesterday: the scout, sent ahead to count the fires and report plainly. Did you give one plain report, nothing added? Day four hundred twenty-three.

There's a fig tree somewhere near you, or a peach tree, or a strawberry patch at a farm stand. For a few weeks each summer the fruit is perfect, and then it's gone. Nobody stands under a bare fig tree in January shouting at it. We know how fruit works. Epictetus thought we forget that knowledge the moment it's a person. In the same long talk where he tells us not to be moved by what isn't ours, book three, chapter twenty-four, he reaches for the fig. Today: in its season.
screen: `A FEW PERFECT WEEKS.` → `NOBODY YELLS AT A BARE TREE.` → `IN ITS SEASON.`

segments.voice: First, the fig in winter. Epictetus says that to long for a friend or a child when they're no longer given to you is like longing for a fig in winter. Not wicked. Just out of season. The tree was never going to give fruit in the snow, and wanting it doesn't change the tree. Second, the kiss. Then he says something that makes people wince. When you kiss your child, he says, you might quietly tell yourself: tomorrow you may die. His listeners objected right away. That's an ill-omened thing to say. Third, his answer. Is it ill-omened, he asks, to say that the grain will be harvested? That leaves fall? That a fresh fig becomes a dried one, and a grape a raisin? These are only changes, things moving from one state to the next. Nothing in nature is cursed by being named. The point of the whisper isn't to spoil the kiss. It's to make it real, to kiss a living person who is here now, rather than a permanent possession you assume you'll always have. Fourth, the gratitude. The same chapter turns this into thanks. Everything we love comes to us, Epictetus says, as something given, for a time, and not forever. So the right response isn't to clutch, and it isn't to stop loving. It's to receive the season while it lasts, and to say thank you when it ends. Other traditions have their own ways of saying it: Ecclesiastes says there is a time for every purpose under heaven. Epictetus says it with a fig.
screen: `A FIG IN WINTER.` · `THE WHISPER DURING THE KISS.` · `NAMING CHANGE IS NOT A CURSE.` · `RECEIVE IT, THEN SAY THANK YOU.` · then, large: `IN ITS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose season with you has changed. A grandparent. A friend from an old job. A teacher. Someone who moved away, or grew up, or died. Picture one ordinary moment with them, the kitchen, the car, the bench. Let yourself feel how good that season was. Now, silently or under your breath, simply say: thank you for that season. If they're still reachable, you might decide now to tell them later today. If not, let the thanks rest where it is. The bell holds the time.
In its season. Epictetus' fig: what we love is given for a time, like fruit, so we receive it while it's here and give thanks when it passes. Today's word.
Your line: in its season. Today, thank one person, out loud or in a message, for the season they've been in your life. Say what it was. Day four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism remind themselves, gently, that the people they love are with them for a time, and use that reminder to be more present and more grateful rather than more anxious.

fork.setup: you're one of Epictetus' students. he's just said to whisper tomorrow you may die while kissing your child. what's your first reaction?
options: that's an ill-omened thing to say.
fork.reveal: his listeners said exactly that. he asked back: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested, or that a fig becomes a dried fig?

trapdoor: what you thought: everything has a season, a nice greeting-card thought.
what it means: Epictetus says what we love is given for a time, so we receive it fully and give thanks when it ends.
what a scholar hears: Discourses 3.24 echoes Enchiridion 3, where Epictetus says that when you kiss your child, remember you are kissing a human being.

notes: Discourses 3.24: the fig in winter, the whisper while kissing a child, the 'ill-omened' objection and the replies about grain, leaves, fig and raisin; paraphrased. Confirm section numbers (roughly 3.24.84–94).
Ecclesiastes 3:1 is paraphrased (KJV wording: 'To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven'), mentioned only as a neighbor, not a comparison.
The gratitude framing ('given for a time') is a fair summary of 3.24's argument that what we have is on loan; confirm emphasis.
